deckName: KS3 DT · J2 Lesson 1 — Welcome to the Workshop (Teacher Deck)

slides.kicker: OUR LADY'S GRAMMAR SCHOOL · DIGITAL TECHNOLOGY
slides.heading: Lesson 1 · Welcome to the Workshop
slides.sub: Your first Digital Technology lesson of the year — J2 · Lesson 1 of 17
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: seated, logged in to the computer, nothing else open. Most of these pupils have never used this website before, and this is their first-ever sign-in to it.

SAY: "Good morning. Books away, hands off the mice, and look up here — this hour starts with me, not with the computers."

WHY: names and eye contact first. The whole of this lesson rests on the class believing that nothing today is a test, and that is easier to establish from the front than to repair later.

WHEN TO MOVE: as soon as the room is settled.

slides.heading: In this lesson you will…
bullets: Find out what your Workshop year is about: you build real things, and you learn how to keep them safe.
Find your way around this website, and see where your work is saved.
Learn the six rules of the DT rooms, then inspect a room and spot the computers where they were broken.
Show what you can do already — the Snapshot is not a test and nobody can fail it.
Finish the big parts of the lesson to earn a reward called a badge, and unlock a new look for your screen.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: still eyes front, screens ignored.

SAY: "Five things today." Then read the five lines out.

WATCH FOR: the fourth line is the one to land hardest. A class that believes the Snapshot counts will guess badly, and the whole value of it is that it is honest.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on.

slides.heading: What The Workshop means
bullets: Your Digital Technology year is called The Workshop, because you work the way a real workshop works.
You BUILD real things: programs that follow your instructions, spreadsheets that work things out for you, and web pages you write yourself.
Then you learn to PROTECT what you build, and to spot the tricks people use to get at other people's work.
Seventeen Workshop lessons this year, one every fortnight.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: eyes front.

SAY: "Two words for the whole year: build, then protect. You make real things, and then you learn how to look after them." Then read the four lines out.

WHY: the pupils' own welcome card says the same thing in the same words a few minutes from now, so this is not a preamble — it is the first hearing of a sentence they are about to read for themselves.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on.

slides.heading: The rules of these rooms
bullets: Never come into the room without a teacher. Line up quietly outside, in single file, until your teacher arrives.
No food and no drink anywhere near the machines.
Look after the equipment. Nothing gets unplugged, moved or taken apart.
Push your chair in and leave your area tidy before you go.
Sign out every time you finish.
Tell your teacher about anything broken, straight away.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: eyes front.

SAY: "These are our six rules, and they are the same in every DT room in the school." Then read all six out.

WHY: deliver them as OUR rules, not the website's. The pupils meet the same six on their own screens later in the hour and then have to spot them being broken, so you are giving them the answers first, on purpose. These are word for word what the pupils will read.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on.

slides.heading: Ready? Go.
bullets: Open Google Classroom, then click the Digital Technology Lesson 1 link.
Read the welcome card together — it types itself out, so wait for the last line.
Then work on your own. The screen gives you five short steps, one at a time.
When a card pops up to say you have finished that part, stop and look up. That card is your badge.
Stuck on the way? Click the round ? button at the bottom right, then put your hand up.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: about to open the website for the first time.

SAY: "Google Classroom first, then the Digital Technology Lesson 1 link. Nothing else." Wait until the room is on the welcome card before you say another word.

THEN SAY: "We are going to read this together." The card types itself out, so wait for the last line, then read it aloud while pupils follow on their own screens. It also explains the Google permission screens they clicked through to get in, so nobody is left wondering what those were.

THEN SAY: "Work through the five steps on your own. When your badge card pops up, stop and look up."

WATCH FOR: if the link is not on Google Classroom, put the QR code from the Classes tab on the board instead. And walk the room — the pupils who need you are the ones who cannot find something on screen.

WHEN TO MOVE: when the first badge cards appear, stop the whole room for the inspection.

slides.heading: Five things to find
bullets: The Year map button at the top left. It takes you back to the page with all seventeen lessons on it — but do not press it yet.
The padlocks on your year map. Nearly every tile has one, and that is normal: each lesson opens on the day you do it.
The small green word Saved at the top right. There is no save button on this website.
The round ? button at the bottom right. It gives you help for the screen you are on.
Your own name at the top right. It opens your Kit Locker, where the new looks for your screen are kept.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: on the second screen of the lesson, working down five short steps.

SAY: "Seven minutes on this now saves you a term of putting your hand up. Each step tells you exactly what to look for."

THEN SAY, pointing at the picture: "The steps come one at a time. You tick the box yourself once you have found the thing, and the next step then appears. There is nothing to hurry."

WATCH FOR: the padlock step. A locked tile looks like a fault to a pupil who has never seen this website, and every tile except today's is locked. Say that one out loud yourself rather than leaving it to the screen.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on to the badge slide while they work.

slides.heading: Badges, points and your Kit Locker
bullets: There are four big parts to this lesson. Finish one and the website gives you a badge — a picture in your own record that says you did it.
Every badge brings points. On the badge card the points are called XP.
Points unlock new looks for your screen, and your looks are kept in your Kit Locker.
Once you have unlocked a look it stays yours for the rest of the year.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: finishing the five steps. The first badge card is appearing on screens around the room.

SAY: "That card is a badge. There are four of them in this hour. Nothing is handed out and nothing is printed — a badge is a picture in your own record on this website, and it comes with points."

WATCH FOR: a pupil who opens the Kit Locker and asks whether that is all there is. On day one it holds three looks — the one that pupil's screen is wearing and the two this lesson can unlock — and the rest arrive as the year unlocks new levels. That pupil is reading it right: it is the beginning of a collection, not the whole of it.

WHEN TO MOVE: when badge cards have appeared around the room, stop everybody.

slides.heading: STOP — eyes front · The Safety Inspection
bullets: You are the safety inspector. You get a drawing of an ICT room just after a class has left it.
Each computer and the space around it is called a station. There are five in the room.
Click a station you think is breaking a rule and a flag goes on it. Click it again and the flag comes off.
Nothing is marked until you press File my inspection report, so change your mind as often as you like.
Talk it over with the pupil beside you — then each of you files your own report.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: first badge earned, screens ignored, eyes front. This is the longest activity of the hour, so the minute you spend here is the minute that makes it work.

SAY: "You are the safety inspector now. You will see a drawing of an ICT room just after a class has left it, with five stations along the bench. A station is one computer and the space around it. Click any station you think is breaking one of our six rules and a flag goes on it. Click it again and the flag comes off. Nothing is judged until you file your report, so change your mind as often as you like — and a flag on a station that turns out to be fine costs you nothing."

THEN SAY, and it is the sentence that decides the quality of the work: "Talk it over with the pupil beside you. You each file your own report, so you do not have to agree."

DO NOT SAY: anything about what is wrong in any of the rooms. The rooms are not on this deck for the same reason — every station in them is an answer.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on to the next slide, then send them in.

slides.heading: What the inspection looks like
bullets: First you get the six rules again, written out, so nobody is guessing.
Then a numbered list of how it works, and a button that says Start the inspection.
Five of the six rules are ones you can SEE in a room. The first one happens outside the door.
You get four goes at it — your screen calls them Scene 1 of 4 to Scene 4 of 4 — then a harder extra challenge you can choose to do or skip.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: about to press into the inspection.

SAY: "The picture on the right is the screen you land on. Rules first, then how it works, then Start the inspection."

THEN SAY: "After the four scenes there is a harder extra challenge. It is genuinely optional — there is a Stop here instead button beside it and nothing is taken off you for pressing it."

WHY: pupils only take an optional challenge if they believe it is optional, so say it rather than leaving it on the screen.

WHILE THEY WORK: circulate. One of the four scenes turns on reading what is actually ON a screen rather than whether it is lit — the brief says which and why, and it is the one place not to help too early.

WHEN TO MOVE: when most of the class has filed the fourth report, stop the room for the Snapshot. Pupils still on the extra challenge can finish it.

slides.heading: STOP — The Skills Snapshot
bullets: Twelve quick questions about what you can do already.
It is NOT a test, you cannot fail it, and nobody is marking it.
Most of it is about things nobody has taught you yet, so not knowing is completely normal.
You will not be told right or wrong, and that is on purpose.
At the end of the year you answer some of them again, and you see the difference for yourself.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: inspection reports filed, facing front.

SAY, and set the tone in one go before anybody starts it: "Quiet and on your own now. Twelve quick questions. It is not a test, you cannot fail it, and I am not marking it. Most of them are about things nobody has taught you yet, so not knowing is completely normal and completely expected. You will not be told right or wrong, and that is deliberate — this is a record of where you are starting from, and it is only worth having if it is honest."

WHY: the thing that ruins a starting-point record is a pupil who thinks it counts, so it is worth saying twice.

IF A PUPIL ASKS WHETHER IT GIVES YOU A SCORE: nothing is marked on a pupil's screen and no pupil is ever told right or wrong. On the staff side you get a picture of how the class answered, and that is for your planning. That is the honest answer and it is the one to give.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on to the next slide, then let them start.

slides.heading: What the Snapshot looks like
bullets: One question at a time, with four answers to choose from.
When you click, the screen says Answer saved and nothing else. That is it working.
There is no right-or-wrong message on these, so there is nothing to compare with anybody.
If you do not know one, pick what seems most likely and keep going.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: about to start twelve questions on their own, in silence.

SAY: "The screen will say Answer saved and nothing else. That is it working, not the website being broken."

WHY: somebody always asks, and answering it once to the whole room saves answering it at desk after desk.

WATCH FOR: the picture on the right is what they will see twelve times over — a question and four answers. The words Answer saved appear where the chosen answer was, a moment after a pupil clicks, and that is the whole of the response.

WHILE THEY WORK: this is the quietest part of the hour and the best chance to catch up with anyone whose sign-in was awkward at the start.

WHEN TO MOVE: when the room has finished.

slides.heading: STOP — The Workshop Warrant
bullets: Your Warrant is your proof that you know your way around the Workshop.
Six questions, and every one of them is about this hour.
Read the reason underneath every answer. It tells you why the answer was right or wrong.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: Snapshot finished, facing front. Tell them this stop is a short one — it is, and saying so keeps the room with you.

SAY: "The Warrant is your proof that you know your way around the Workshop. Six questions, all of them about this hour — nothing from outside it. Read the reason underneath every answer, every single time."

WHY: the reason under a marked answer is the teaching, and pupils will click past it if nobody tells them not to. It is the one habit worth establishing in the first hour of the year.

WHEN TO MOVE: straight on.

slides.heading: What the Warrant looks like
bullets: A card tells you what the Warrant is. Then the six questions start.
Click an answer and the screen tells you straight away whether you were right, with a short reason underneath.
After the sixth question a badge lands, and your first new look is waiting on your year map.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: about to start the Warrant.

SAY: "The picture on the right is the card that opens it. Then six questions that behave the way the earlier ones did."

THEN SAY: "The new look is not inside the lesson. It appears when you get back to your year map at the end."

WHY: otherwise the pupils who finish first go hunting for it inside the lesson.

WHILE THEY WORK: the Live tab shows how the class did question by question. Anything most of the room got wrong is worth a sentence to everybody rather than a conversation at every desk.

WHEN TO MOVE: when the badge cards have landed.

slides.heading: What you build next
bullets: One card before you finish, so you know where the year is going.
Next comes From Blocks to Python — four lessons long.
The first of them is Lesson 2, Translation Bureau, and it starts from your very first line of Python.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: Warrant done, reading one card on their own.

SAY: "One card about what you build next, then two screens and we are finished."

WHY: nobody should leave the first hour of the year not knowing where it is going. The card names the block and the next lesson, and says plainly that nothing is assumed.

WHEN TO MOVE: as soon as the card is confirmed.

slides.heading: The last two screens
bullets: One question, on your own. This one IS marked, so think about it.
You find out how you did right at the end, after the last screen.
Then How did it go?, where you say honestly how the hour went.
The comment box goes to your teacher and nobody else. Everyone finishes this screen before leaving.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: working through the last two screens on their own.

SAY: "One question now, on your own, and this one is marked — so think about it. You find out how you did right at the end, after the last screen, so do not sit waiting for an answer."

THEN SAY: "Then tell me honestly how today went. The comment box comes to me and nobody else."

WATCH FOR: the picture on the right is the final screen — three sentences to rate, a how-it-felt choice and a comment box.

NOBODY LEAVES WITHOUT FINISHING How did it go? It is compulsory, and it is how you hear from the pupils who never put a hand up. The staff panel flags any pupil who answers Not yet, so a quiet pupil having a hard time reaches you without having to say so out loud.

WHEN TO MOVE: when both screens are done.

slides.heading: Before you leave
bullets: Sign out every time. If you stay signed in, anything the next person does on this computer looks like you did it.
Chair in, area tidy, nothing left beside your machine.
Next time: From Blocks to Python, starting with Lesson 2, Translation Bureau.
slides.notes:
WHERE THE CLASS IS: finished, packing up.

SAY: "Two jobs before you stand up. Sign out — if you stay signed in, anything the next person does on this computer looks like you did it. Then chair in, area tidy, nothing left beside your machine."

WHY: the class has just spent the biggest part of the hour flagging other people's untidy stations, so this is the moment those two rules land.

WHEN TO MOVE: dismiss when the room is signed out and tidy.
